A joint I could build and revise

The actuator sets the limits of the whole robot: torque, speed, stiffness, heat, and packaging all meet at the joint.

I developed cycloidal actuator assemblies using parametric CAD and FDM fabrication. Repeated prototypes helped me work through disk and pin geometry, bearings, shafts, tolerances, and assembly. The original 17:1 design became a starting point for a revised 25:1 version with greater torque margin.

Design and manufacturing decisions

I used prototype results to revisit clearances, bearing selection, print orientation, and the mechanical interfaces between the reducer, motor, and robot leg. Separate bills of materials document the 17:1 and 25:1 assemblies, including their different output-shaft sleeve bearings.

Ideal reduction relationships
ωout = ωmotor / G
τout ≈ η G τmotor

G is the reduction ratio and η is drivetrain efficiency. More reduction increases available output torque for a given motor torque while reducing output speed. Actual output depends on losses, heat, and the motor operating point.

Inertia reflected to the motor
Jload → motor = Jload / G²

This ideal relationship describes load inertia seen at the motor. Motor inertia reflected to the output follows the opposite scaling, Jmotor · G²; a higher reduction can therefore affect joint responsiveness.

Building a way to measure

I developed a dynamometer layout and used fixture tests to examine torque, efficiency, backlash, stiffness, durability, and thermal behavior. These tests helped distinguish a geometry that assembled successfully from a joint that behaved usefully under load.

I keep the test conditions attached to the data. A plotted result can guide a revision without establishing a continuous torque or lifetime rating.

An evolving actuator platform

PROJECT STATUS

Built prototypes, published CAD, and a revised reduction.

Printed actuators were integrated into the quadruped prototype. The repository retains the original 17:1 design and documents a revised 25:1 assembly; the original version is no longer maintained. Motor development uses an ST development board and Berkeley Humanoid Lite / Recoil firmware. Custom-board bring-up remains a separate project.
